Appendix H. The Sequence Toolbox

H-1. Summation Formulas

Key points in 3 lines

  1. The sum of an arithmetic sequence is “number of terms × (average of the first and last terms),” and the sum of a geometric sequence is “(first term − the term after the last)/(1 − common ratio).”

  2. Sums of powers (k², k³) can be derived directly by “folding with differences” and by induction, so there is no need to memorize them.

  3. A geometric sum with a factor of k attached is solved in one stroke by “S − rS.”

H-1-1. Gauss’s Sum: Three Proofs

Claim. 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2.

Proof ① (adding backwards). Add S = 1 + 2 + … + n and S = n + (n−1) + … + 1 position by position. Each pair sums to n+1 and there are n pairs, so 2S = n(n+1).

Proof ② (folding with differences, that is, the telescoping of H-3). Add (k+1)² − k² = 2k + 1 over k = 1, …, n. On the left the middle terms all cancel, leaving (n+1)² − 1; on the right we get 2S + n. Hence 2S = n² + 2n − n = n(n+1). (This method is generalized in H-1-3.)

Proof ③ (induction). For n = 1, 1 = 1·2/2. If it holds for n, then n(n+1)/2 + (n+1) = (n+1)(n+2)/2. (Induction is the subject of H-2.)

Anecdote. The story that the young Gauss instantly answered 5050 for the sum from 1 to 100 is famous. The details vary from edition to edition, so we present it only as “a story that has been handed down.” The mathematical content is nothing more than ① above.

H-1-2. Sums of Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences

Arithmetic. With first term a₁, common difference d, and terms aₙ = a₁ + (n−1)d,

Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2 = n(2a₁ + (n−1)d)/2.

The proof is the same as adding backwards. The reason is that the sum of the k-th term from the front and the k-th term from the back, aₖ + aₙ₊₁₋ₖ, is always a₁ + aₙ.

Geometric. With first term a and common ratio r ≠ 1,

Sₙ = a + ar + … + arⁿ⁻¹ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r).

Proof. Sₙ − r·Sₙ = a − a·rⁿ, so (1 − r)Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ). Since r ≠ 1 we may divide. If r = 1, then Sₙ = na.

Infinite geometric series. If |r| < 1, then rⁿ → 0, so the sum is a/(1 − r). If a ≠ 0 and |r| ≥ 1, the series does not converge.

Proof that rⁿ → 0. If |r| < 1, we can write |r| = 1/(1 + x) with x > 0. By Bernoulli’s inequality (H-2, Example 4), (1 + x)ⁿ ≥ 1 + nx, so |r|ⁿ ≤ 1/(1 + nx) → 0. Also, keeping only the first three terms of the binomial expansion gives (1 + x)ⁿ ≥ 1 + nx + n(n−1)x²/2, so n|r|ⁿ ≤ n/(1 + nx + n(n−1)x²/2) → 0 (we use this in H-1-5).

Why the series diverges when |r| ≥ 1. If the series converged, its general term arⁿ⁻¹, which is the difference of consecutive partial sums, would have to go to 0. But if a ≠ 0 and |r| ≥ 1, then |arⁿ⁻¹| ≥ |a|, so it does not go to 0.

Example. A ball dropped from 10 m bounces back each time to 0.9 times the previous height. The total distance traveled is 10 + 2(9 + 8.1 + 7.29 + …) = 10 + 2·9/(1 − 0.9) = 190 m. (9 is the first rebound height and 0.9 is the common ratio.) Looking separately at 9 + 8.1 + 7.29 + … alone, the sum is 90.

Connection to recurrences. Expanding aₙ₊₁ = r·aₙ + c out n times gives aₙ = rⁿa₀ + c(1 + r + … + rⁿ⁻¹), and the parenthesis is a geometric sum. If r ≠ 1, then with the fixed point a* = c/(1 − r) we get aₙ = a* + (a₀ − a*)rⁿ.

H-1-3. Sums of Powers

Claim.

  • Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6

  • Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k³ = (n(n+1)/2)²

Derivation for k² (folding with differences). Add (k+1)³ − k³ = 3k² + 3k + 1 over k = 1, …, n:

(n+1)³ − 1 = 3·Σk² + 3·n(n+1)/2 + n.

To leave only 3·Σk², move n and 3n(n+1)/2 to the left side:

3·Σk² = (n+1)³ − 1 − n − 3n(n+1)/2.

Simplifying the right side gives n³ + 3n² + 2n − (3n² + 3n)/2 = (2n³ + 3n² + n)/2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/2, so Σk² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.

Proof for k³ (induction). For n = 1, 1 = 1². Suppose it holds for n. Then

(n(n+1)/2)² + (n+1)³ = (n+1)²(n²/4 + n + 1) = (n+1)²(n+2)²/4 = ((n+1)(n+2)/2)².

Check. n = 3: 1 + 4 + 9 = 14 = 3·4·7/6, and 1 + 8 + 27 = 36 = 6².

Sum of squares of odd numbers. Σₖ₌₁ⁿ (2k−1)² = n(2n−1)(2n+1)/3. Expanding gives 4k² − 4k + 1, so the sum is 4·n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 − 4·n(n+1)/2 + n = n(4n² − 1)/3. n = 3: 1 + 9 + 25 = 35 = 3·5·7/3.

Generalization. Sₚ(n) = Σₖ₌₁ⁿ kᵖ is a polynomial of degree p+1 in n, and its leading term is n^(p+1)/(p+1).

Proof (induction on p). Add (k+1)^(p+1) − k^(p+1) = Σ(i=0..p) C(p+1, i)·kⁱ over k = 1, …, n. The left side telescopes, giving

(n+1)^(p+1) − 1 = Σ(i=0..p) C(p+1, i)·Sᵢ(n) (S₀(n) = n).

The i = p term is (p+1)·Sₚ(n), so

Sₚ(n) = [ (n+1)^(p+1) − 1 − Σ(i=0..p−1) C(p+1, i)·Sᵢ(n) ] / (p+1).

By the induction hypothesis, each Sᵢ(n) with i < p is a polynomial of degree i+1 ≤ p or lower, so on the right side the degree-(p+1) term comes only from (n+1)^(p+1), and its coefficient is 1/(p+1) ≠ 0. Hence Sₚ(n) is a polynomial of exactly degree p+1. ∎

The formula that gives all the coefficients at once is Faulhaber’s formula, which uses the Bernoulli numbers Bⱼ (with the convention B₁ = +1/2):

Sₚ(n) = (1/(p+1))·Σ(j=0..p) C(p+1, j)·Bⱼ·n^(p+1−j).

(A rigorous proof that a formula of this form holds for every p was completed by Jacobi (1834).) It is enough to be able to derive up to about p ≤ 3 from the recursion above; beyond that, just look up the formula when you need it.

Proof of Faulhaber’s formula (optional reading). The Bernoulli numbers are defined by the formal power series t/(eᵗ − 1) = Σⱼ₌₀^∞ Bⱼ·tʲ/j! (B₀ = 1, B₁ = −1/2, B₂ = 1/6, …). Let Tₚ(n) = Σₖ₌₀^(n−1) kᵖ. Then

Σₖ₌₀^(n−1) e^(kt) = (e^(nt) − 1)/(eᵗ − 1) = [(e^(nt) − 1)/t]·[t/(eᵗ − 1)].

On the left, the coefficient of tᵖ/p! is Tₚ(n). On the right, the first factor is Σₘ n^(m+1)·tᵐ/(m+1)!, so the coefficient of tᵖ on the right is Σ(j=0..p) [n^(p+1−j)/(p+1−j)!]·[Bⱼ/j!]. Multiplying both sides by p! and using p!/((p+1−j)!·j!) = C(p+1, j)/(p+1), we get

Tₚ(n) = (1/(p+1))·Σ(j=0..p) C(p+1, j)·Bⱼ·n^(p+1−j) (B₁ = −1/2).

Since Σₖ₌₁ⁿ kᵖ = Tₚ(n) + nᵖ and the j = 1 term is B₁·nᵖ, adding nᵖ is the same as changing B₁ = −1/2 to +1/2. ∎ (Check: for p = 2, (1/3)[n³ + 3·(1/2)·n² + 3·(1/6)·n] = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.)

Binomial-coefficient version (hockey stick). Σₖ₌ₘⁿ C(k, m) = C(n+1, m+1). From Pascal’s identity C(k+1, m+1) = C(k, m+1) + C(k, m) we get C(k, m) = C(k+1, m+1) − C(k, m+1). Summing over k = m, …, n, the sum telescopes to C(n+1, m+1) − C(m, m+1) = C(n+1, m+1). (The case m = 2 is the binomial-coefficient item in H-3-4.)

H-1-4. Difference Sequences

If we know the difference sequence bₖ = aₖ₊₁ − aₖ of a sequence (aₙ), then

aₙ = a₁ + Σₖ₌₁ⁿ⁻¹ bₖ.

Proof. Adding bₖ over k = 1, …, n−1 leaves only the two ends (the telescoping principle of H-3).

Example. The sequence 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, … has differences 1, 2, 3, 4, …, so aₙ = 1 + (1 + 2 + … + (n−1)) = 1 + n(n−1)/2. (This is the same sequence as the maximum number of regions into which n−1 lines divide a plane. With n lines it is 1 + n(n+1)/2 = aₙ₊₁.) For n = 5, a₅ = 1 + 10 = 11 (the number of regions made by 4 lines).

Rule of thumb. If the difference sequence is arithmetic (with nonzero common difference), the general term is a quadratic; if the difference sequence is a quadratic, the general term is a cubic. Remember that “each time you take a difference, the degree drops by one,” and you can handle polynomial-type sequences quickly. (Reason: for the leading term c·kᵈ, (k+1)ᵈ − kᵈ = d·kᵈ⁻¹ + (lower-degree terms), so the difference of a degree-d polynomial is a degree-(d−1) polynomial whose leading coefficient is dc ≠ 0. Conversely, the sum of a degree-(d−1) polynomial becomes a degree-d polynomial by the method of H-1-3.)

H-1-5. Arithmetico-Geometric Sums: Σ k·rᵏ

A geometric sum with a factor of k attached is solved by the S − rS technique. Below we take r ≠ 1 (for r = 1, Σk = n(n+1)/2).

Let S = Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k·rᵏ. Then rS = Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k·rᵏ⁺¹ = Σₖ₌₂ⁿ⁺¹ (k−1)·rᵏ. Subtracting, the coefficient of rᵏ becomes k − (k−1) = 1, so

(1 − r)S = Σₖ₌₁ⁿ rᵏ − n·rⁿ⁺¹.

For r = 2. −S = (2ⁿ⁺¹ − 2) − n·2ⁿ⁺¹, that is,

Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k·2ᵏ = (n − 1)·2ⁿ⁺¹ + 2.

For r = 3. Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k·3ᵏ = ((2n − 1)·3ⁿ⁺¹ + 3)/4.

Check. n = 3, r = 2: 2 + 8 + 24 = 34 = 2·16 + 2. n = 3, r = 3: 3 + 18 + 81 = 102 = (5·81 + 3)/4 = 408/4.

Infinite sum. If |r| < 1, then n·rⁿ⁺¹ → 0 (use n|r|ⁿ → 0 shown in H-1-2), and Σₖ₌₁ⁿ rᵏ = r(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) → r/(1 − r), so (1 − r)S → r/(1 − r), that is, Σₖ₌₁^∞ k·rᵏ = r/(1 − r)². (Example: for r = 1/2 it is 2.)

H-1-6. Examples (Easy → Standard → Challenging)

Example 1. The sum of the first 20 terms of 3, 7, 11, …. The common difference is 4, a₂₀ = 3 + 19·4 = 79, and S₂₀ = 20·(3 + 79)/2 = 820.

Example 2. Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k(k+1) = n(n+1)(n+2)/3.

Since k(k+1) = k² + k, the sum is n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 + n(n+1)/2 = n(n+1)(2n+1+3)/6 = n(n+1)(n+2)/3. n = 3: 2 + 6 + 12 = 20 = 3·4·5/3.

Example 3 (challenging). Find Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k(k+1)(k+2).

Expanding gives k³ + 3k² + 2k, so it can be solved with the three formulas of H-1-3, but the computation is long. The insight: a product of three consecutive numbers can be written as “the difference between it and the next consecutive product.” The answer is n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)/4, and H-3-3 proves it in one line. n = 2: 6 + 24 = 30 = 2·3·4·5/4.

H-1-7. Pitfalls

  • Number of terms: From the m-th term to the n-th term there are n − m + 1 terms. If you count “n − m,” you are one short.

  • r = 1 in a geometric sum: Plugging into the formula divides by zero. Handle it separately.

  • Convergence condition for infinite sums: Do not use a/(1 − r) without checking |r| < 1.

  • Starting index: Depending on whether it is Σₖ₌₀ⁿ or Σₖ₌₁ⁿ, there is one term of difference.

  • The last term of S − rS: The most common mistake is to drop the leftover −n·rⁿ⁺¹ term after subtracting. Always check with n = 1. For n = 1, S = r and (1 − r)S = r − r² = Σₖ₌₁¹ rᵏ − 1·r², which is correct.

H-2. Mathematical Induction

Key points in 3 lines

  1. Induction = “the first domino falls (base case) + whenever any domino falls, the next one falls too (step).”

  2. In the step, you must use the hypothesis, and you must check that the step’s argument is valid for every n (especially the value right after the base case).

  3. If you get stuck, prove a stronger statement. The hypothesis becomes stronger along with it.

The “verification” and “proof” parts of recurrence problems are almost all finished with this tool.

H-2-1. The Principle

If a statement P(n) satisfies the following two conditions, then P(n) is true for every natural number n.

  1. Base case: P(1) is true.

  2. Inductive step: If P(n) is true for some n, then P(n+1) is also true.

The domino analogy. If the first domino falls (base case), and every domino falls whenever the one before it falls (step), then all of them fall.

Why it is correct (the least counterexample). Suppose the set S of values of n for which the statement is false is not empty. The set of natural numbers has the property that “every nonempty subset has a minimum” (well-ordering), so S has a minimum m. If m = 1, this contradicts the base case. If m > 1, then m − 1 ∉ S, so P(m−1) is true, and by the inductive step P(m) is also true, contradicting m ∈ S. Therefore S is empty.

A correct way to write it up

  • State the claim P(n) explicitly in one sentence.

  • Show the base case by actually computing it.

  • Write “Assume P(n) is true,” and then be sure to use that assumption somewhere. If you did not use the assumption, either induction was not needed or the proof is wrong.

  • In the conclusion, state how far you have proved it (n ≥ 1 or n ≥ 4).

H-2-2. Basic Examples

Example 1 (a summation formula). 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n−1) = n².

Base: for n = 1, 1 = 1². Step: if it holds for n, then n² + (2n+1) = (n+1)². (Picture an n×n square with an L-shaped band wrapped around it.)

Example 2 (verifying the solution of a recurrence). If aₙ₊₁ = 2aₙ + 1 and a₁ = 1, then aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1.

Base: a₁ = 1 = 2¹ − 1. Step: if aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1, then aₙ₊₁ = 2(2ⁿ − 1) + 1 = 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 1. (This is the same recurrence as the minimum number of moves in the Tower of Hanoi.)

Example 3 (divisibility). For every n ≥ 1, 5ⁿ − 1 is a multiple of 4.

Base: 5 − 1 = 4. Step: 5ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 = 5(5ⁿ − 1) + 4, and since 5ⁿ − 1 is a multiple of 4, the whole right side is a multiple of 4.

(Tip: split the new expression into “a multiple of the expression the hypothesis handles + a remainder you can check.”)

Example 4 (an inequality, Bernoulli). If x ≥ −1 and n ≥ 1, then (1 + x)ⁿ ≥ 1 + nx.

Base: for n = 1, equality. Step: (1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹ = (1 + x)(1 + x)ⁿ ≥ (1 + x)(1 + nx) = 1 + (n+1)x + nx² ≥ 1 + (n+1)x. In the first inequality, 1 + x ≥ 0 was used (you must multiply by a nonnegative number for the inequality to be preserved). This is the reason for the condition x ≥ −1.

Example 5 (2ⁿ and n²). If n ≥ 4, then 2ⁿ ≥ n².

Base: for n = 4, 16 ≥ 16. Step: 2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2·2ⁿ ≥ 2n², and if n ≥ 3, then n² ≥ 2n + 1, so 2n² ≥ n² + 2n + 1 = (n+1)². (Note that the base case starts at 4. For n = 3, 8 < 9, so it is in fact false.)

Example 6 (divisibility that skips two steps). For every n ≥ 1, 3²ⁿ⁺² − 8n − 9 is a multiple of 64.

Let f(n) = 3²ⁿ⁺² − 8n − 9. Base: f(1) = 81 − 8 − 9 = 64. Step: f(n+1) − 9·f(n) = (−8n − 8 − 9) − 9(−8n − 9) = 64n + 64. Hence f(n+1) = 9f(n) + 64(n + 1), and if f(n) is a multiple of 64, then f(n+1) is too.

(Tip: choose the constant c so that f(n+1) − c·f(n) becomes “an expression you can check.” Here c = 9.)

H-2-3. Strong Induction

Here the induction hypothesis is strengthened from just “P(n)” to “all of P(1), P(2), …, P(n).” It is natural for recurrences that look back two or more terms, and for problems that “break n into smaller numbers.” Logically it has the same power as the basic form (apply the basic form to Q(n) = “P(1)∧…∧P(n)”).

Example 7 (an upper bound for Fibonacci). If F₁ = F₂ = 1 and Fₙ₊₁ = Fₙ + Fₙ₋₁, then Fₙ < 2ⁿ.

Two base cases are needed. n = 1: 1 < 2; n = 2: 1 < 4. Step (n ≥ 2): Fₙ₊₁ = Fₙ + Fₙ₋₁ < 2ⁿ + 2ⁿ⁻¹ < 2ⁿ + 2ⁿ = 2ⁿ⁺¹. (If the recurrence looks back two terms, there are also two base cases. This is the same story as the order of a recurrence determining the number of initial values.)

Example 8 (the postage stamp problem). We have only 3-won and 5-won stamps. Every integer amount of 8 won or more can be made.

Base: 8 = 3 + 5, 9 = 3 + 3 + 3, 10 = 5 + 5. Step: if n ≥ 11, then n − 3 ≥ 8, so by the hypothesis n − 3 can be made, and adding one 3-won stamp gives n. There are three base cases because the step “goes back 3 places.”

(Remark: 7 won cannot be made, so 8 is exactly the boundary. In general, for two coprime positive integers a, b, the largest amount that cannot be made is ab − a − b (Sylvester). Examples: for 4 and 7 it is 17; for 5 and 8 it is 27.)

Proof (Sylvester). Since gcd(a, b) = 1, by Bézout’s identity every integer n can be written in the form n = ax + by (x, y integers), and by adding a multiple of b to x and subtracting a multiple of a from y, we can arrange 0 ≤ x ≤ b−1. The x in this range is unique (from a(x − x′) = b(y′ − y) we get b | (x − x′)). Then

  • n can be made with nonnegative integer coefficients ⟺ y ≥ 0 in the representation above. (If it can be made, then n = ax′ + by′ with x′, y′ ≥ 0, and writing x′ = x + bt (t ≥ 0), we get y = y′ + at ≥ 0.)

  • If n = ab − a − b = a(b−1) + b·(−1), then x = b−1 and y = −1 < 0, so it cannot be made.

  • If n > ab − a − b, then ax ≤ a(b−1), so by = n − ax > −b, that is, y > −1. Since y is an integer, y ≥ 0, and it can be made. ∎

H-2-4. Backward Induction (Cauchy’s Induction)

This is a structure that “proves the statement for infinitely many n, then comes back down and fills in the rest.”

  1. P(2) is true.

  2. P(n) ⇒ P(2n). (Then it is true for n = 2, 4, 8, 16, …)

  3. P(n) ⇒ P(n−1). (Then all the gaps are filled.)

Example 9 (the AM–GM inequality). For positive reals x₁, …, xₙ, (x₁ + … + xₙ)/n ≥ (x₁⋯xₙ)^(1/n).

  • P(2): (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab) is equivalent to (√a − √b)² ≥ 0.

  • P(n) ⇒ P(2n): Let A and G₁ be the arithmetic and geometric means of the first n numbers, and B and G₂ those of the last n. By P(n), A ≥ G₁ and B ≥ G₂. The arithmetic mean of all 2n numbers is (A + B)/2 ≥ √(AB) ≥ √(G₁G₂). But G₁G₂ = (the whole product)^(1/n), so its square root is (the whole product)^(1/(2n)), which is the geometric mean of the 2n numbers.

  • P(n) ⇒ P(n−1): Let m be the arithmetic mean of x₁, …, xₙ₋₁, and apply P(n) to the n numbers x₁, …, xₙ₋₁, m. The arithmetic mean of these n numbers is ((n−1)m + m)/n = m, so m ≥ (x₁⋯xₙ₋₁·m)^(1/n). Raising both sides to the n-th power and dividing by m gives mⁿ⁻¹ ≥ x₁⋯xₙ₋₁. Taking the (n−1)-th root of both sides gives P(n−1).

Wrapping up. By step 2, P(2ᵏ) is true for every k (induction on k). For any n, choose k with 2ᵏ ≥ n, and starting from P(2ᵏ), apply step 3 repeatedly (2ᵏ − n) times to obtain P(n).

It is good to know this as a shift in thinking for solving problems where the step from n to n+1 is blocked.

H-2-5. “Strengthening” Induction: Prove a Stronger Statement

The paradox of induction: sometimes a stronger statement is easier to prove. This is because the induction hypothesis becomes stronger as well.

Example 10. For every n ≥ 1, 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + … + 1/n² < 2.

Induction as it stands gets stuck. Adding 1/(n+1)² to the hypothesis “sum < 2” gives “< 2 + a positive number,” so we cannot obtain “< 2.” So we prove a stronger statement that depends on n.

P(n): Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/k² ≤ 2 − 1/n.

Base: for n = 1, 1 ≤ 1. Step: by the hypothesis, the sum is ≤ 2 − 1/n + 1/(n+1)². It suffices to show that this is at most 2 − 1/(n+1). That is, 1/(n+1)² ≤ 1/n − 1/(n+1) = 1/(n(n+1)), which is true because n(n+1) ≤ (n+1)². Hence the sum is ≤ 2 − 1/n < 2.

(In H-3-4 we obtain the same inequality again as a telescoping series. Exercise C10 asks you to prove the better upper bound 5/3 − 2/(2n+1) in the same way.)

H-2-6. Anatomy of Common Errors in Induction

Fake proof 1: “All horses are the same color”

Claim. If there are n horses, they are all the same color.

“Proof.” Base n = 1: a single horse is of course the same color. Step: assume that any n horses are all the same color. Given n + 1 horses, remove one horse, and the remaining n horses are the same color; remove a different horse, and again the remaining n horses are the same color. Since there is a horse that belongs to both groups, all of them are the same color.

What is wrong. In the step from n = 1 to n = 2, “a horse that belongs to both groups” does not exist. If you remove one of the two horses, the remaining horse is A, and if you remove the other, the remaining horse is B, and A and B are different horses. For there to be an overlapping horse, we need n − 1 ≥ 1, that is, n ≥ 2. In other words, the inductive-step argument is invalid at n = 1, and this was not checked.

How to check. Confirm that the argument of the inductive step is valid for every n (including the value right after the base case). In particular, for small values such as n = 1, 2, examine whether the “overlap,” “splitting,” or “removal” that the argument uses is actually possible.

Fake proof 2: Induction with no base case

P(n): “n = n + 1.” The inductive step is valid. If n = n+1, adding 1 to both sides gives n+1 = n+2. But P(1) is false, so there is no base case. The step alone proves nothing.

Fake proof 3: “Induction” that does not use the induction hypothesis

If you write “Assume it holds for n. Computing directly at n+1 …” and never use the assumption even once, then it is simply a direct proof, and if direct computation is in fact impossible for general n, it is a wrong proof.

Other items to check

  • Number of base cases: As many as the number of places the step looks back (Examples 7, 8).

  • Validity of “n+1 objects → remove one → n objects”: Check that an arbitrary collection of n+1 objects can in fact be obtained this way, and that the n objects left after removal satisfy the conditions of the hypothesis. The opposite direction (”add one object to n objects”) is dangerous because it may not produce every collection of (n+1) objects.

  • Confusion with “true for large n”: Watch out for the mistake of rewriting “for every n” as “for sufficiently large n.”

H-3. Telescoping Series and Summation Techniques

Key points in 3 lines

  1. If you can put the term in the form aₖ = f(k) − f(k+1), the sum leaves only the two ends. The problem is finding f.

  2. For fractions, partial fractions; for products, products of consecutive integers; for square roots, rationalization is the key.

  3. If the gap is m, m terms remain at each end. For infinite sums, do not forget to check the limit of the tail.

H-3-1. The Core Principle

Theorem. For any sequence b₁, b₂, …,

Σₖ₌₁ⁿ (bₖ − bₖ₊₁) = b₁ − bₙ₊₁.

Proof. Writing out the terms gives (b₁ − b₂) + (b₂ − b₃) + … + (bₙ − bₙ₊₁), and the middle terms cancel in pairs. (Rigorously, by induction on n: for n = 1 it is b₁ − b₂; if it holds for n, then b₁ − bₙ₊₁ + (bₙ₊₁ − bₙ₊₂) = b₁ − bₙ₊₂.) ∎

Infinite sum. If bₙ → L, then Σₖ₌₁^∞ (bₖ − bₖ₊₁) = b₁ − L.

This is the same story as the difference sequence of H-1-4, told from the opposite direction.

H-3-2. Partial Fractions

A fraction whose denominator is a product of distinct linear factors is split into a sum of fractions.

Basic form. 1/(k(k+m)) = (1/m)·(1/k − 1/(k+m)). (Over a common denominator, (k+m−k)/(k(k+m)) = m/(k(k+m)), which confirms it.)

Example 1. Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/(k(k+1)) = 1 − 1/(n+1) = n/(n+1), and the infinite sum is 1.

Example 2 (skipping two places). Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/(k(k+2)) = ½ Σ (1/k − 1/(k+2)).

This time two terms remain at each end. The 1 and 1/2 at the front have no partners to cancel with, and neither do −1/(n+1) and −1/(n+2) at the back.

= ½(1 + 1/2 − 1/(n+1) − 1/(n+2)). The infinite sum is ½·(3/2) = 3/4.

Check: for n = 2, 1/3 + 1/8 = 11/24, and the formula gives ½(3/2 − 1/3 − 1/4) = ½·(11/12) = 11/24.

In general: if the gap is m, m terms remain. Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/(k(k+m)) = (1/m)(1 + 1/2 + … + 1/m − 1/(n+1) − … − 1/(n+m)). The infinite sum is (1/m)(1 + 1/2 + … + 1/m). For m = 3 it is 11/18. (Exercise B2)

A quick way to find the coefficients (the cover-up method). In 1/(k(k+m)) = A/k + B/(k+m), A is “what is left after covering k and putting in k = 0,” namely 1/(0+m) = 1/m, and B is “what is left after covering (k+m) and putting in k = −m,” namely 1/(−m) = −1/m. (Reason: multiplying both sides by k gives 1/(k+m) = A + Bk/(k+m), and putting k = 0 in this gives A = 1/m.) If the linear factors are all distinct, the same method gives each coefficient in one step even with three or more factors.

H-3-3. Telescoping with Products of Consecutive Integers

Idea. The difference of products of r consecutive integers k(k+1)…(k+r−1) is

k(k+1)…(k+r) − (k−1)k…(k+r−1) = (r+1)·k(k+1)…(k+r−1).

(Factoring out the common factor k(k+1)…(k+r−1) leaves [(k+r) − (k−1)] = r+1.) So if we set f(k) = k(k+1)…(k+r)/(r+1), then k(k+1)…(k+r−1) = f(k) − f(k−1), and since f(0) = 0, the sum is f(n).

Results.

  • Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k = n(n+1)/2 (r = 1)

  • Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k(k+1) = n(n+1)(n+2)/3 (r = 2)

  • Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k(k+1)(k+2) = n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)/4 (r = 3)

  • Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k(k+1)(k+2)(k+3) = n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)(n+4)/5 (r = 4)

The answer to the challenge in H-1-6, Example 3 comes out in one line. Check for n = 2: 6 + 24 = 30 = 2·3·4·5/4.

Reciprocal version. 1/(k(k+1)(k+2)) = ½[1/(k(k+1)) − 1/((k+1)(k+2))]. Hence

Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/(k(k+1)(k+2)) = ½[1/2 − 1/((n+1)(n+2))], and the infinite sum is 1/4.

Check: for n = 1, 1/6, and the formula gives ½(1/2 − 1/6) = 1/6.

In the same way, 1/(k(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)) = (1/3)[1/(k(k+1)(k+2)) − 1/((k+1)(k+2)(k+3))] (over a common denominator the numerator is (k+3) − k = 3), so Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/(k(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)) = 1/18 − 1/(3(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)), and the infinite sum is 1/18. Check for n = 1: 1/24 = 1/18 − 1/72.

H-3-4. Other Telescoping Patterns

Each line goes in the order “term → folded form → sum.”

  • Factorial. k·k! = (k+1)! − k! → Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k·k! = (n+1)! − 1.

  • Reciprocal factorial. k/(k+1)! = 1/k! − 1/(k+1)! → the sum is 1 − 1/(n+1)!.

  • Square root. 1/(√k + √(k+1)) = √(k+1) − √k → the sum is √(n+1) − 1.

  • Product form 1. 1 + 1/k = (k+1)/k, so Πₖ₌₁ⁿ (1 + 1/k) = n + 1.

  • Product form 2. 1 − 1/k² = (k−1)(k+1)/k², so Πₖ₌₂ⁿ (1 − 1/k²) = (n+1)/(2n).

  • Binomial coefficients. C(k, 2) = C(k+1, 3) − C(k, 3) → Σₖ₌₁ⁿ C(k, 2) = C(n+1, 3).

  • Arctangent. arctan(1/(k²+k+1)) = arctan(k+1) − arctan k → the sum is arctan(n+1) − π/4.

  • A term mixed with factorials. k!(k² + k + 1) = (k+1)(k+1)! − k·k! → Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k!(k²+k+1) = (n+1)(n+1)! − 1.

Checks.

  • Σₖ₌₁³ k·k! = 1 + 4 + 18 = 23 = 4! − 1.

  • Σₖ₌₁³ k/(k+1)! = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/8 = 23/24 = 1 − 1/24.

  • Πₖ₌₂³ (1 − 1/k²) = 3/4 · 8/9 = 2/3 = 4/6.

  • Binomial coefficients: for n = 4, C(2,2) + C(3,2) + C(4,2) = 1 + 3 + 6 = 10 = C(5,3). This identity comes directly from C(k+1,3) − C(k,3) = C(k,2) in Pascal’s triangle, and it is the case m = 2 of the hockey-stick identity in H-1-3.

  • Arctangent: tan[arctan(k+1) − arctan k] = ((k+1) − k)/(1 + k(k+1)) = 1/(k²+k+1), so it holds. (The two angles arctan(k+1) − arctan k and arctan(1/(k²+k+1)) both lie in (0, π/2), and tan is one-to-one on this interval, so if their tan values are equal, the angles are equal.)

  • A term mixed with factorials: for n = 2, 3 + 14 = 17 = 3·6 − 1.

Rationalizing a square-root term. Multiplying the numerator and denominator of 1/(√k + √(k+1)) by (√(k+1) − √k) makes the denominator (k+1) − k = 1, giving √(k+1) − √k. “If the denominator is irrational, rationalize it and it will fold” is the signal.

Reproving H-2-5, Example 10. For k ≥ 2, 1/k² < 1/(k(k−1)) = 1/(k−1) − 1/k, so Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/k² < 1 + (1 − 1/n) = 2 − 1/n. This is shorter than induction.

H-3-5. An Advanced Example Where the Denominator Factors

Example 3. Find Σₙ₌₁^∞ n/(n⁴ + n² + 1).

Factor the denominator: n⁴ + n² + 1 = (n² + 1)² − n² = (n² − n + 1)(n² + n + 1). Meanwhile, (n² + n + 1) − (n² − n + 1) = 2n, so

n/(n⁴ + n² + 1) = ½ [1/(n² − n + 1) − 1/(n² + n + 1)].

Since n² − n + 1 = (n−1)² + (n−1) + 1, if we let g(m) = 1/(m² + m + 1), the term is ½[g(n−1) − g(n)]. Hence the partial sum is ½[g(0) − g(n)] = ½[1 − 1/(n² + n + 1)], and the infinite sum is 1/2. Check: for n = 1, 1/3, and the formula gives ½(1 − 1/3) = 1/3.

H-3-6. The Harmonic Series Does Not Fold (It Diverges)

Σ 1/k is not a “folding” sum. Instead, we show divergence by grouping and pressing down (Oresme’s method).

In H(2ᵐ) = 1 + 1/2 + (1/3 + 1/4) + (1/5 + … + 1/8) + …, the j-th group (1/(2ʲ⁻¹+1) + … + 1/2ʲ) consists of 2ʲ⁻¹ terms each at least 1/2ʲ, so its sum is at least 1/2. Hence H(2ᵐ) ≥ 1 + m/2 → ∞.

Lesson. Even among terms of the same 1/k form, 1/(k(k+1)) converges (it folds) while 1/k diverges. That the terms go to 0 is not by itself enough to guarantee convergence.

H-3-7. Transforming Sums

Interchanging the order of a double sum. Σₖ₌₁ⁿ Σⱼ₌₁ᵏ j can be counted in two ways.

  • Outer k first: Σₖ₌₁ⁿ k(k+1)/2 = n(n+1)(n+2)/6.

  • With j on the outside: j appears once for each k with j ≤ k ≤ n, that is, (n − j + 1) times, so the sum is Σⱼ₌₁ⁿ j(n − j + 1).

The fact that the two expressions are equal lets the formulas of H-1 verify one another. n = 3: 1·3 + 2·2 + 3·1 = 10 = 3·4·5/6.

Abel transformation (moving to partial sums). Letting Aₖ = a₁ + … + aₖ,

Σₖ₌₁ⁿ aₖbₖ = Aₙbₙ + Σₖ₌₁ⁿ⁻¹ Aₖ(bₖ − bₖ₊₁).

Proof. Substituting aₖ = Aₖ − Aₖ₋₁ (A₀ = 0) gives Σ(Aₖ − Aₖ₋₁)bₖ = ΣAₖbₖ − ΣAₖ₋₁bₖ. Shifting the index of the second sum gives Σₖ₌₁ⁿ⁻¹ Aₖbₖ₊₁, and rearranging yields the formula above. It has the same structure as integration by parts, and it is useful for estimating sums when one of the sequences is monotone.

H-3-8. A Checklist for Building a Telescoping Series

  1. If the term is a fraction, factor the denominator and split it into partial fractions.

  2. If the term is a product, suspect products of consecutive integers (k(k+1)…) or a factorial form.

  3. If the term has a √, rationalize it.

  4. If a recurrence is involved, try turning the recurrence itself into a difference (the last example of H-5).

  5. Guess an f such that f(k) − f(k+1) = the term, and verify by computing the difference directly.

  6. After folding, count how many terms remain, and recheck the index range.

  7. For an infinite sum, confirm that the limit of the remaining tail exists.

H-3-9. Pitfalls

  • Number of leftover terms: If the gap is m, m terms remain at the front and m at the back (Example 2). The most common mistake is to imagine that only one remains.

  • Trusting cancellation without checking the limit: 1 − 1 + 1 − 1 + … can be grouped as (1−1) + (1−1) + … = 0 or as 1 + (−1+1) + … = 1, so the sum is not defined. For telescoping to be valid, the limit of the partial sum b₁ − bₙ₊₁ as n → ∞ must exist.

  • Shifting indices: If you change k to k+1 and do not change the range of the sum along with it, the terms are off by one.

  • Zero denominators: Check that no k in the range of the sum makes a denominator of the partial fractions zero.

H-4. Integrality and Remainder Rules

Key points in 3 lines

  1. “Does this sequence produce only integers?” is solved by one of (a) converting it to an integer-coefficient linear recurrence, (b) conjugate pairs, or (c) counting.

  2. For a division recurrence, once you find an invariant, it is proved to be the same as a linear recurrence.

  3. A sequence of remainders has only finitely many states, so it must enter a cycle. If the recurrence can be run backwards, it is periodic from the very beginning.

H-4 explains things using only the phrase “the remainder on division by m,” without the congruence symbol (≡). If the symbol is more convenient for you, feel free to rewrite the text with it.

H-4-1. The Question: Does This Sequence Produce Only Integers?

For a linear recurrence aₙ₊₂ = p·aₙ₊₁ + q·aₙ (p, q integers) with integer initial values and integer coefficients, every term is an integer by induction (the sum and product of two integers are integers). The following three cases are where it gets harder.

  1. The recurrence involves division.

  2. The general term is written with irrational numbers (Binet’s formula, etc.).

  3. The terms are given only by a combinatorial definition.

H-4-2. Method ①: Turning a Division Recurrence into a Linear Recurrence

Problem. If a₀ = a₁ = 1 and aₙ₊₁ = (aₙ² + 2)/aₙ₋₁, is every aₙ an integer?

Attempt. Computing directly, a₂ = 3, a₃ = (9 + 2)/1 = 11, a₄ = (121 + 2)/3 = 41, a₅ = (1681 + 2)/11 = 153. The divisions seem to come out even. But it is not clear “why” they always do.

Observation. The numbers 1, 1, 3, 11, 41, 153 satisfy aₙ₊₁ = 4aₙ − aₙ₋₁ (4·3 − 1 = 11, 4·11 − 3 = 41, 4·41 − 11 = 153).

Plan of the proof. Define a new sequence (bₙ) by the integer linear recurrence bₙ₊₁ = 4bₙ − bₙ₋₁, b₀ = b₁ = 1.

  • (bₙ) is a sequence of integers.

  • (bₙ) is entirely positive. By induction: if bₙ, bₙ₋₁ > 0 and bₙ ≥ bₙ₋₁, then bₙ₊₁ = 4bₙ − bₙ₋₁ ≥ 3bₙ > bₙ. So it is increasing and positive.

  • We show that (bₙ) also satisfies the original fractional recurrence bₙ₊₁ = (bₙ² + 2)/bₙ₋₁ (below).

  • The original sequence is uniquely determined by its initial values and recurrence (since the divisor is never 0), so aₙ = bₙ. Hence every aₙ is an integer.

Key lemma (an invariant). Qₙ = bₙ² + bₙ₋₁² − 4bₙbₙ₋₁ is a constant, −2, independent of n.

  • Q₁ = 1 + 1 − 4 = −2.

  • In Qₙ₊₁ = bₙ₊₁² + bₙ² − 4bₙ₊₁bₙ, group the first and last terms: bₙ₊₁² − 4bₙ₊₁bₙ = bₙ₊₁(bₙ₊₁ − 4bₙ) = −bₙ₊₁bₙ₋₁ = −(4bₙ − bₙ₋₁)bₙ₋₁ = −4bₙbₙ₋₁ + bₙ₋₁². Hence Qₙ₊₁ = bₙ² + bₙ₋₁² − 4bₙbₙ₋₁ = Qₙ.

Conclusion. From Qₙ = −2, bₙ² + 2 = 4bₙbₙ₋₁ − bₙ₋₁² = bₙ₋₁(4bₙ − bₙ₋₁) = bₙ₋₁bₙ₊₁. That is, bₙ₊₁ = (bₙ² + 2)/bₙ₋₁.

Generalization (2 or 3 cases). There is nothing special about the numbers 4 and 2 in the proof above. For a positive integer k, every term of

aₙ₊₁ = (aₙ² + k)/aₙ₋₁, a₀ = a₁ = 1

is an integer. The integer recurrence is bₙ₊₁ = (k+2)bₙ − bₙ₋₁, and the invariant is Qₙ = bₙ² + bₙ₋₁² − (k+2)bₙbₙ₋₁ = −k (Q₁ = 2 − (k+2) = −k). Exactly as in the previous proof, we get bₙ² + k = bₙ₋₁bₙ₊₁. The proof of positivity is the same, using bₙ₊₁ = (k+2)bₙ − bₙ₋₁ ≥ (k+1)bₙ > 0.

  • k = 1: 1, 1, 2, 5, 13, 34, … (the recurrence is aₙ₊₁ = 3aₙ − aₙ₋₁. For n ≥ 1, aₙ = F₂ₙ₋₁, that is, it is the same sequence as the odd-indexed Fibonacci terms F₁, F₃, F₅, …. Exercise B12)

  • k = 2: 1, 1, 3, 11, 41, 153, … (the main text above)

  • k = 3: 1, 1, 4, 19, 91, … (the recurrence is aₙ₊₁ = 5aₙ − aₙ₋₁. Exercise C4)

Generalized lesson. To show that “a sequence defined by a fraction is integer-valued,” (1) guess an integer recurrence from the first few terms, and (2) find an invariant to show that the two recurrences are the same. This kind of “miracle of integrality” generalizes to the Somos sequences and others, but this appendix covers only the technique above.

H-4-3. Method ②: Making Integers with Conjugates

Theorem. For every n ≥ 0, cₙ = (2 + √3)ⁿ + (2 − √3)ⁿ is an even integer, and for n ≥ 1, the ceiling of (2 + √3)ⁿ is cₙ and the floor is cₙ − 1 (odd).

Proof.

(a) The two numbers 2 ± √3 are the roots of x² − 4x + 1 = 0 (sum 4, product 1). So xⁿ⁺² = 4xⁿ⁺¹ − xⁿ holds for both roots, and adding them gives cₙ₊₂ = 4cₙ₊₁ − cₙ.

(b) c₀ = 2, c₁ = 4. Since this is a recurrence with integer coefficients, every cₙ is an integer, and since the first two terms are even, by induction every cₙ is even (cₙ₊₂ = 4cₙ₊₁ − cₙ is even − even). The first terms: 2, 4, 14, 52, 194, ….

(c) Since 0 < 2 − √3 < 1, for n ≥ 1 we have 0 < (2 − √3)ⁿ < 1. Hence (2 + √3)ⁿ = cₙ − (2 − √3)ⁿ is greater than cₙ − 1 and less than cₙ. That is, the ceiling is cₙ and the floor is cₙ − 1.

Check. n = 1: 2 + √3 ≈ 3.732 → ceiling 4 = c₁. n = 2: (2 + √3)² = 7 + 4√3 ≈ 13.93 → ceiling 14 = c₂.

Meaning. It is the same structure as the phenomenon in Binet’s formula where ψⁿ/√5 is small, so rounding gives a Fibonacci number. “An integer recurrence with irrational roots + a conjugate between 0 and 1” is a regular subject.

If the conjugate is negative, the sign alternates. cₙ = (1 + √2)ⁿ + (1 − √2)ⁿ is also an integer (c₁ = 2, c₂ = 6, c₃ = 14, …, cₙ₊₂ = 2cₙ₊₁ + cₙ), but 1 − √2 ≈ −0.414 is negative, so the sign of (1 − √2)ⁿ is (−1)ⁿ. Therefore, when n is odd, (1 + √2)ⁿ = cₙ − (a negative number of absolute value < 1) is greater than cₙ, so the floor is cₙ, not cₙ − 1; when n is even, it is less than cₙ, so the floor is cₙ − 1. Examples: for n = 1, the floor of 2.414… is 2 = c₁; for n = 2, the floor of 5.828… is 5 = c₂ − 1.

Another example. (3 + √5)ⁿ can be solved the same way. 3 ± √5 are the roots of x² − 6x + 4 = 0, and 3 − √5 ≈ 0.76 lies between 0 and 1, so cₙ = (3 + √5)ⁿ + (3 − √5)ⁿ is an integer (c₀ = 2, c₁ = 6, and since cₙ₊₂ = 6cₙ₊₁ − 4cₙ, all are even), and the floor of (3 + √5)ⁿ is cₙ − 1, which is odd. (Exercise B13)

H-4-4. Method ③: Showing Integrality by Counting

If a sequence is “the count of something,” integrality comes for free. The recurrence for the Catalan numbers, Cₙ₊₁ = 2(2n + 1)/(n + 2) · Cₙ, contains a fraction and so looks as if it might not give integers, but since Cₙ is the number of ways to match parentheses correctly, it is an integer. (It can also be shown directly from the recurrence side. Dₙ = C(2n, n)/(n+1) = C(2n, n) − C(2n, n+1) is the difference of two integers, so it is an integer; D₀ = 1; and from C(2n+2, n+1) = C(2n, n)·2(2n+1)/(n+1) we get Dₙ₊₁ = 2(2n+1)/(n+2)·Dₙ. Since the initial value and the recurrence are the same, Cₙ = Dₙ, which is an integer. Example: C₃ = 20 − 15 = 5.) That the binomial coefficient C(n, k) = C(n−1, k−1) + C(n−1, k) is an integer follows immediately from induction and Pascal’s recurrence.

H-4-5. Remainder Rule I: The Period of the Last Digit

For the last digit of a power, it is enough to track only “the remainder on division by 10” as you multiply. This is because the last digit is the only information that determines the next term.

  • Base 2: 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, … period 4

  • Base 3: 3, 9, 7, 1, 3, … period 4

  • Base 7: 7, 9, 3, 1, 7, … period 4

  • Base 4: 4, 6, 4, … period 2

  • Base 9: 9, 1, 9, … period 2

Examples. The last digit of 7²⁰²⁴: 2024 is a multiple of 4, so it is the last value of the period, 1. The last digit of 3¹⁰⁰: 100 is a multiple of 4, so 1. 3²⁰²⁵ + 7²⁰²⁵: since 2025 = 4·506 + 1, the last digits are 3 and 7, and the last digit of the sum is 0.

H-4-6. Remainder Rule II: A Sequence Must Enter a Cycle

Theorem. Suppose an integer sequence has the form aₙ₊₂ = f(aₙ₊₁, aₙ) with f a polynomial with integer coefficients. The sequence of remainders rₙ on division by m eventually becomes periodic (after discarding a few initial terms, the cycle repeats). In particular, when it is also determined backwards (for example, for aₙ₊₂ = p·aₙ₊₁ + q·aₙ, if q and m are coprime, then aₙ = (aₙ₊₂ − p·aₙ₊₁)/q can be computed on the remainders modulo m), it is periodic from the very beginning.

Proof (i): eventually periodic. The state sₙ = (rₙ, rₙ₊₁) is one of m² possibilities, and the next state sₙ₊₁ is determined by the current state sₙ alone. Among s₀, s₁, …, s_{m²} there are m² + 1 states, so by the pigeonhole principle there exist i < j with sᵢ = sⱼ. Since the next state is determined by the current state, sᵢ₊ₜ = sⱼ₊ₜ (for all t ≥ 0), that is, from the i-th term on, it repeats with period j − i.

Proof (ii): if it is also determined backwards, periodic from the start. Let X be the set of all states (m² elements), and T the map sending a state to the next state. That it is determined backwards means T is injective (different states do not go to the same place), and an injective map on a finite set is bijective, so T⁻¹ exists. For the starting state s₀, by (i) there exist i < j with Tⁱ(s₀) = Tʲ(s₀). Applying T⁻¹ i times to both sides, s₀ = Tʲ⁻ⁱ(s₀). That is, it returns to s₀ itself, so it is periodic from the start.

(Note: without the condition of (ii), the initial segment may not enter the cycle. Example: for x₀ = 2, xₙ₊₁ = xₙ², the last digits are 2, 4, 6, 6, 6, …, and the initial 2, 4 never appear again.)

Upper bound on the period. Since there are m² states, the period is at most m². In particular, for a homogeneous linear recurrence such as aₙ₊₂ = p·aₙ₊₁ + q·aₙ, in which (0, 0) goes only back to itself, the period of any start other than (0, 0) is at most m² − 1. The actual period is often much shorter.

Remainders of Fibonacci (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …).

  • Remainders mod 2: 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, … period 3. So Fₙ is even ⟺ n is a multiple of 3.

  • Remainders mod 3: 1, 1, 2, 0, 2, 2, 1, 0, 1, 1, … period 8. Zero appears at positions 4, 8, …, so Fₙ is a multiple of 3 ⟺ n is a multiple of 4. (F₄ = 3, F₈ = 21)

  • Remainders mod 5: period 20, and zero appears at positions 5, 10, 15, 20. So Fₙ is a multiple of 5 ⟺ n is a multiple of 5.

  • Remainders mod 4: Fₙ is a multiple of 4 ⟺ n is a multiple of 6. (F₆ = 8, F₁₂ = 144)

  • The period of the remainders mod 10 is 60 (the Pisano period).

(All of these facts can be confirmed by directly computing one full cycle. Because of (ii), checking a single cycle settles the whole sequence. Incidentally, in general gcd(Fₘ, Fₙ) = F_gcd(m, n) holds (proved in H-4-8), and from this the rules for dividing by 2, 3, 5 follow immediately (F₃ = 2, F₄ = 3, F₅ = 5). Since 4 is not a Fibonacci number, the mod 4 rule is the result of directly checking the period 6.)

H-4-7. Remainder Rule III: Linear Congruential Sequences (LCG)

If we view aₙ₊₁ = r·aₙ + c through the remainder on division by m, it is the same object as the linear congruential generator (LCG) used as a computer random number generator. It is a one-step recurrence, and if r and m are coprime it is reversible, so by H-4-6 (ii) it is periodic from the very beginning.

The necessary and sufficient condition for the period to be m (the maximum) is known as the Hull–Dobell theorem (T. E. Hull, A. R. Dobell, SIAM Review 4, 1962; a proof is also in Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 2, Section 3.2.1.2): (1) c and m are coprime, (2) r − 1 is divisible by every prime factor of m, (3) if m is a multiple of 4, then r − 1 is also a multiple of 4. For example, for m = 16, r = 5, we have r − 1 = 4, so (2) and (3) are satisfied, and when c is odd the period is 16. For r = 3, r − 1 = 2 is not a multiple of 4, so the period cannot be 16.

Proof of the Hull–Dobell theorem (optional reading). That the period is m means that x₀, x₁, …, xₘ₋₁ are all distinct and xₘ = x₀. In that case all m residue classes appear exactly once, so the map x ↦ rx + c is a cycle that goes around all m states in one loop, and the period is m regardless of the starting value. So we may take the starting value to be 0.

Necessity. Suppose the period is m. The sequence repeats every m terms from the beginning, and every residue class appears.

  1. If a prime p divides both c and m, then mod p we have xₙ₊₁ ≡ r·xₙ and x₀ = 0, so xₙ ≡ 0 only, and 1 mod p can never appear. Hence gcd(c, m) = 1.

  2. Suppose a prime p | m and r ≢ 1 (mod p). Since 1 − r is not divisible by p, there is a fixed point x* mod p (x* ≡ r·x* + c). Since every residue class appears, at some n we have xₙ ≡ x* (mod p), and all later terms are x* mod p. But there is a residue class y (mod m) different from x* mod p (since p ≥ 2), and y must reappear every m steps, a contradiction. Hence r ≡ 1 (mod p).

  3. Suppose 4 | m and r ≢ 1 (mod 4). By item 2, r is odd, so r ≡ 3 (mod 4), and by item 1, c is odd. Since xₙ₊₂ = r²xₙ + (r+1)c ≡ xₙ (mod 4), the sequence mod 4 repeats with period at most 2 and cannot produce all four residue classes. Contradiction.

Sufficiency. Suppose (1)–(3) hold. If r = 1, then xₙ = nc, which is trivial, so take a representative r ≥ 2. If x₀ = 0, then xₙ = c·Sₙ with Sₙ = 1 + r + … + rⁿ⁻¹ = (rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1). Since c is coprime to m, xₙ ≡ 0 (mod m) ⟺ Sₙ ≡ 0 (mod m). So it suffices to show Sₙ ≡ 0 (mod m) ⟺ m | n, because then the first return to 0 is at n = m, and the proof is complete. With the prime factorization m = Πpᵉ, it is enough to show for each p that Sₙ ≡ 0 (mod pᵉ) ⟺ pᵉ | n. (The Chinese remainder theorem.)

  • If e = 1, then r ≡ 1 (mod p), so Sₙ ≡ n (mod p), and we are done.

  • If e ≥ 2 (when p = 2, r ≡ 1 (mod 4) by item 3), we show that v(Sₙ) = v(n) for the p-adic valuation v(·).

    • n = p: Write r = 1 + d with p | d (4 | d if p = 2). Since (1 + d)ⁱ ≡ 1 + id (mod d²), Sₚ ≡ p + d·p(p−1)/2 (mod d²). If p is odd, both d·p(p−1)/2 and d² are multiples of p², so Sₚ ≡ p (mod p²). If p = 2, S₂ = 2 + d ≡ 2 (mod 4). Either way, v(Sₚ) = 1.

    • Product structure: S_{uv}(r) = S_u(r)·S_v(rᵘ) ((r^{uv} − 1)/(r − 1) = (rᵘ − 1)/(r − 1) · (r^{uv} − 1)/(rᵘ − 1)). Since rᵘ is also congruent to 1 mod p (mod 4 if p = 2), the result above applies to rᵘ as well.

    • n = pᵏ: Since S_{pᵏ⁺¹}(r) = S_{pᵏ}(r)·S_p(r^{pᵏ}), v increases by one each time, so v(S_{pᵏ}) = k.

    • General n = pᵏ·s (p ∤ s): Sₙ = S_{pᵏ}(r)·S_s(r^{pᵏ}), and since r^{pᵏ} ≡ 1 (mod p), S_s(r^{pᵏ}) ≡ s ≢ 0 (mod p). Hence v(Sₙ) = k = v(n). ∎

A direct proof for m = 16, r = 5. It can be checked even without the theorem above. If c is even, the values starting from 0 stay even forever, so they cannot pass through all 16 residue classes. If c is odd, then from x₀ = 0 we get xₙ = c(1 + 5 + … + 5ⁿ⁻¹) = c(5ⁿ − 1)/4, and since c is coprime to 16, xₙ ≡ 0 (mod 16) ⟺ 5ⁿ ≡ 1 (mod 64). By induction one can show that 5^(2ʲ) = 1 + 2^(j+2)·(an odd number) ((1 + 2^(j+2)u)² = 1 + 2^(j+3)(u + 2^(j+1)u²), and if u is odd the parenthesis is also odd), so 5⁸ = 1 + 2⁵·(an odd number) has remainder other than 1 mod 64, while 5¹⁶ ≡ 1 (mod 64). Since 5¹⁶ ≡ 1, the order of 5 divides 16, and since 5⁸ ≢ 1, it is exactly 16, so the orbit of 0 covers all 16 residue classes. This map is a permutation, so the period is 16 for every starting value.

H-4-8. Other Tools for Proving Integrality

  • Integer by induction: A linear recurrence with integer coefficients gives integers (H-4-1).

  • Invariants: Some combination of the recurrence is a constant independent of n (Qₙ in H-4-2).

  • Conjugate pairs: Sums of powers of a root and its conjugate (H-4-3).

  • Combinatorial interpretation: It is a count, so it is an integer (H-4-4).

  • Proof of coprimality: gcd(Fₙ₊₁, Fₙ) = gcd(Fₙ, Fₙ₋₁) = … = gcd(F₂, F₁) = 1. (Euclidean algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a − b). Since Fₙ₊₁ − Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁, gcd(Fₙ₊₁, Fₙ) = gcd(Fₙ, Fₙ₋₁).)

  • gcd(Fₘ, Fₙ) = F_gcd(m, n). Setting F₀ = 0, the identity Fₘ₊ₙ = Fₘ₋₁Fₙ + FₘFₙ₊₁ (m ≥ 1, n ≥ 0) holds. (Induction on m: for m = 1, Fₙ₊₁ = F₀Fₙ + F₁Fₙ₊₁; for m = 2, Fₙ₊₂ = F₁Fₙ + F₂Fₙ₊₁. If it holds for m−1 and m, then Fₘ₊₁₊ₙ = Fₘ₊ₙ + Fₘ₋₁₊ₙ = (Fₘ₋₁Fₙ + FₘFₙ₊₁) + (Fₘ₋₂Fₙ + Fₘ₋₁Fₙ₊₁) = FₘFₙ + Fₘ₊₁Fₙ₊₁.) If a > b, this identity gives Fₐ = Fₐ₋ᵦ₋₁Fᵦ + Fₐ₋ᵦFᵦ₊₁, so gcd(Fₐ, Fᵦ) = gcd(Fₐ₋ᵦFᵦ₊₁, Fᵦ) = gcd(Fₐ₋ᵦ, Fᵦ). (Since gcd(Fᵦ₊₁, Fᵦ) = 1, the factor Fᵦ₊₁ can be discarded.) This has the same shape as the subtraction step of the Euclidean algorithm, so repeating until the two indices are equal gives gcd(Fₐ, Fᵦ) = F_gcd(a, b). In particular, for m ≥ 3, Fₘ | Fₙ ⟺ m | n. (F is strictly increasing from F₂ on, so F_gcd(m, n) = Fₘ ⟺ gcd(m, n) = m.)

H-4-9. Pitfalls

  • Showing only “integer” by induction without checking “positive”: In H-4-2, bₙ > 0 is needed for the division recurrence to be defined.

  • Two initial values are needed but only one is checked: Trusting the recurrence without checking the integrality of the second term.

  • Guessing from “the period looks short”: If you guessed a period from the first few terms, you must confirm it with a proof (the state repeats).

  • Confusing ceiling/floor with integer part: In H-4-3(c), the key point is that (2 − √3)ⁿ lies between 0 and 1, but if the conjugate is negative (such as 1 − √2), the ceiling and floor swap depending on the sign.

  • The period of a non-reversible recurrence: Saying “periodic from the start” without the condition of (ii) (reversibility) is wrong.

H-5. Worked Solutions to Classic Problems

Key points in 3 lines

  1. When you see a problem, first choose the tool by the shape of the terms: fractions → telescoping; division recurrence → invariant; “for all n” → induction; “divisibility / coprimality” → integer combination (producing the form ax + by = 1) and remainders.

  2. All the problems below are classic problems whose sources can be verified (the International Mathematical Olympiad, the Putnam, and so on), and the solutions were written directly using only the tools of this appendix.

  3. After solving, always check with small n.

Policy on quoting problems. The problems are paraphrased, and the source is noted briefly at the end of each problem. The solutions are my own. Details of the sources and the verification records are gathered at the end of the appendix.

Solution H-5-1. A Coprimality Proof (IMO 1959, Problem 1)

Problem. Show that for every natural number n, the fraction (21n + 4)/(14n + 3) cannot be reduced any further.

Solution. Look for an integer combination of the numerator and denominator. 3(14n + 3) − 2(21n + 4) = 42n + 9 − 42n − 8 = 1. Hence a common divisor d of the two numbers divides the left side of this equation, so it also divides 1. So d = 1.

Another solution (the Euclidean algorithm). gcd(21n+4, 14n+3) = gcd(7n+1, 14n+3) = gcd(7n+1, 1) = 1. This is because (14n+3) − 2(7n+1) = 1.

Check. n = 1: 25/17, gcd 1. n = 2: 46/31, gcd 1.

Tool: Integer combination. If you find integers x, y with ax + by = 1, a common divisor divides 1, so gcd = 1. (The same idea as the Euclidean algorithm in H-4-8.)

Source. The 1st International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO), 1959, Problem 1.

Solution H-5-2. Is a Division Recurrence Integer-Valued? (Moscow Mathematical Olympiad, 1963)

Problem. Show that every term of the sequence defined by a₁ = a₂ = 1, aₙ = (aₙ₋₁² + 2)/aₙ₋₂ (n ≥ 3) is a positive integer.

Solution. This is the case k = 2 of H-4-2 (with the index shifted by one). Define the integer linear recurrence bₙ = 4bₙ₋₁ − bₙ₋₂ (b₁ = b₂ = 1). The invariant bₙ² + bₙ₋₁² − 4bₙbₙ₋₁ = −2 is preserved, giving bₙ² + 2 = bₙ₋₁bₙ₊₁. So (bₙ) satisfies the given recurrence, and since the recurrence is uniquely determined by the initial values, aₙ = bₙ. It is an integer and an increasing sequence, so it is positive.

Addendum. It also follows that all terms are odd: in bₙ = 4bₙ₋₁ − bₙ₋₂, 4bₙ₋₁ is even, so if bₙ₋₂ is odd then bₙ is odd (induction).

Check. 1, 1, 3, 11, 41, 153, 571, …

Source. The 26th Moscow Mathematical Olympiad (1963), upper grades.

Solution H-5-3. Determining a Function from an Inequality Condition (IMO 1977, Problem 6)

Problem. Let f be a function from the positive integers to the positive integers such that f(n+1) > f(f(n)) for every n. Show that f(n) = n.

Solution (induction, strengthening the statement to “for all m ≥ n”).

Step 1: f(m) ≥ n (m ≥ n). P(n): “if m ≥ n, then f(m) ≥ n.” For n = 1 it is true because f takes positive integer values. Suppose P(n) is true. If m ≥ n + 1, then m − 1 ≥ n, so by P(n), f(m−1) ≥ n. Applying P(n) again to the number f(m−1) (which is ≥ n), we get f(f(m−1)) ≥ n. By the condition of the problem, f(m) > f(f(m−1)) ≥ n, so f(m) ≥ n + 1. P(n+1) holds.

Step 2: f is increasing. Putting m = n in Step 1, f(m) ≥ m for every m. Applying this to the number f(n), f(f(n)) ≥ f(n). Hence f(n+1) > f(f(n)) ≥ f(n), that is, f is strictly increasing.

Step 3: f(n) ≤ n. Suppose that for some n, f(n) ≥ n + 1. Since f is increasing, f(f(n)) ≥ f(n+1). This contradicts f(n+1) > f(f(n)). Hence f(n) ≤ n.

Conclusion. From f(n) ≥ n (Step 1) and f(n) ≤ n (Step 3), f(n) = n. Conversely, f(n) = n satisfies the condition, since n + 1 > n.

Source. The 19th IMO, 1977, Problem 6.

Tool: Induction, H-2-5 (first set up a stronger statement).

Solution H-5-4. Telescoping + Factoring (AIME 2002 I, Problem 4)

Problem. Let aₖ = 1/(k² + k) (k ≥ 1). For positive integers m < n with aₘ + aₘ₊₁ + … + aₙ₋₁ = 1/29, find m + n.

Solution. Since aₖ = 1/(k(k+1)) = 1/k − 1/(k+1), the sum telescopes to 1/m − 1/n = 1/29. Multiplying both sides by 29mn gives 29n − 29m = mn, that is, mn + 29m − 29n = 0. Subtracting 29² from both sides and rearranging gives (m − 29)(n + 29) = −29², that is, (29 − m)(29 + n) = 29² = 841.

Since 29 is prime, the positive divisors of 841 are only 1, 29, and 841. Since 29 + n > 29, we have 29 + n = 841 and 29 − m = 1. Hence n = 812, m = 28, and m + n = 840.

Check. 1/28 − 1/812 = (29 − 1)/812 = 28/812 = 1/29.

Source. 2002 AIME I, Problem 4.

Tool: H-3-2 partial fractions, and “convert to product form and count divisors” (the coprimality/divisor argument).

Solution H-5-5. Partial Fractions + Approximation (AIME 2002 II, Problem 6)

Problem. Find the integer closest to 1000·Σₙ₌₃^10000 1/(n² − 4).

Solution. 1/(n² − 4) = 1/((n−2)(n+2)) = ¼(1/(n−2) − 1/(n+2)) (the gap is 4, so four terms remain at the front and four at the back).

Σₙ₌₃^10000 = ¼(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 − 1/9999 − 1/10000 − 1/10001 − 1/10002).

Multiplying by 1000 gives 250(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4) − 250(1/9999 + 1/10000 + 1/10001 + 1/10002) = 520 + 5/6 − r. Here r = 250(the sum of the last four terms), and 0 < r < 250·4/9999 < 1/3. Hence the value 520 + 5/6 − r lies between 520 + 1/2 and 520 + 5/6, and the closest integer is 521.

Check. 250(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4) = 250·25/12 = 520.8333….

Source. 2002 AIME II, Problem 6.

Tool: “If the gap is m, m terms remain at each end” from H-3-2. This problem tests that pitfall (H-3-9) head-on.

Solution H-5-6. When an Infinite Product Telescopes (Putnam 1977, B1)

Problem. Find the value of the infinite product Πₙ₌₂^∞ (n³ − 1)/(n³ + 1).

Solution. Since n³ − 1 = (n − 1)(n² + n + 1) and n³ + 1 = (n + 1)(n² − n + 1),

(n³ − 1)/(n³ + 1) = [(n − 1)/(n + 1)] · [(n² + n + 1)/(n² − n + 1)].

Let g(m) = m² + m + 1. Since n² − n + 1 = (n−1)² + (n−1) + 1 = g(n − 1), the second factor is g(n)/g(n−1). The partial products are

Πₙ₌₂^N (n−1)/(n+1) = (1·2)/(N(N+1)) = 2/(N(N+1)), Πₙ₌₂^N g(n)/g(n−1) = g(N)/g(1) = (N² + N + 1)/3.

Multiplying them, P_N = 2(N² + N + 1)/(3N(N+1)) → 2/3 (N → ∞).

Proof of the partial-product formula (induction). Just because the first few terms seem to cancel does not mean it holds for every N, so we verify. N = 2: the product of (n−1)/(n+1) is 1/3 = 2/(2·3), and g(2)/g(1) = 7/3. If it holds for N, the new factor multiplied in at N+1 is N/(N+2), so 2/(N(N+1))·N/(N+2) = 2/((N+1)(N+2)), and g(N)/g(1)·g(N+1)/g(N) = g(N+1)/g(1). ∎

Check. N = 2: 7/9. The formula gives 2·7/(3·6) = 14/18 = 7/9.

Source. The 38th William Lowell Putnam Competition (1977), B1.

Tool: Telescoping of the product form in H-3-4, and checking the partial-product formula by induction.

Solution H-5-7. Turning the Recurrence Itself into a Difference

Problem. If a₁ = 3/2 and aₙ₊₁ = aₙ² − aₙ + 1, find the value of Σₙ₌₁^∞ 1/aₙ.

Solution. Rewrite the recurrence as aₙ₊₁ − 1 = aₙ(aₙ − 1). Then 1/(aₙ₊₁ − 1) = 1/(aₙ(aₙ − 1)) = 1/(aₙ − 1) − 1/aₙ, that is,

1/aₙ = 1/(aₙ − 1) − 1/(aₙ₊₁ − 1).

(A folding form comes out directly from the recurrence.) Summing, Σₙ₌₁^N 1/aₙ = 1/(a₁ − 1) − 1/(a_(N+1) − 1) = 2 − 1/(a_(N+1) − 1). Since aₙ₊₁ − aₙ = (aₙ − 1)² ≥ 0, the sequence (aₙ) is increasing and at least a₁ = 3/2, so aₙ₊₁ − aₙ ≥ 1/4; hence aₙ → ∞ and the tail 1/(aₙ₊₁ − 1) → 0. The sum is 2.

Check. a₁ = 3/2, a₂ = 7/4, a₃ = 37/16, a₄ = 1033/256. Checking the folded expression: 1/a₁ = 2/3 = 1/(a₁−1) − 1/(a₂−1) = 2 − 4/3. The sum of three terms is 2/3 + 4/7 + 16/37 = 1298/777, and the formula 2 − 1/(a₄ − 1) = 2 − 256/777 = 1298/777.

Generalization. If a₁ = a > 1, the same method gives the sum 1/(a − 1).

Source. Binghamton University Problem of the Week, Fall 2021, No. 6.

Tool: Item 4 of the H-3 checklist (turn the recurrence itself into a difference). By the same method, if a₁ = 2 the sequence is 2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, … (each term is the product of the previous terms plus 1), and Σ 1/aₖ = 1 − 1/(aₙ₊₁ − 1) → 1 (Exercise C3).
